source: Silver et al. (2017) Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play with a General RL Algorithm
finding: AlphaZero beat Stockfish in a 100-game match with 1 minute per move and lost no games.
numbers: 100 games, 1 min/move, Stockfish at strongest level, 64 threads, 1GB hash; AlphaZero lost 0 to Stockfish, 8 to Elmo in shogi.
limits: Stockfish settings and time control were criticised as handicapping it; one fixed protocol. This paper cannot say if the margin holds under other conditions.
agent_relevance: Search gains come from a learned prior and value, not from more nodes alone.

source: Silver et al. (2017) Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play with a General RL Algorithm
finding: AlphaZero searched about 900 times fewer positions than Stockfish and still won, because the network focused the search.
numbers: 80 thousand positions/s (chess), 40 thousand (shogi) versus 70 million (Stockfish), 35 million (Elmo). Beat Stockfish after 4 hours (300k steps).
quote: AlphaZero compensates for the lower number of evaluations by using its deep neural network to focus much more selectively
limits: Hardware was not equal (TPUs vs CPUs), so compute parity is debatable.
agent_relevance: S6 tree search should be narrow and guided by a strong proposal and value, not wide and blind.

source: Silver et al. (2017) Mastering Chess and Shogi by Self-Play with a General RL Algorithm
finding: MCTS scaled better with thinking time than alpha-beta in the paper's Elo-versus-time plot, calling into question the belief that alpha-beta is superior.
numbers: Figure 2: Elo versus thinking time per move, relative to 40ms Stockfish or Elmo.
limits: Only a plot and a claim; a footnote notes draws compress the chess Elo scale. Later results with Stockfish NNUE were not opened this session.
agent_relevance: Do not assume more branches beat deeper selective lines; test the scaling curve on our own task.

source: Schrittwieser et al. (2020) MuZero: Mastering Atari, Go, Chess and Shogi by Planning with a Learned Model
finding: MuZero matched AlphaZero in chess, shogi and Go with no rules given, searching over a learned model; in Go it slightly exceeded AlphaZero with less compute per node.
numbers: Training: 1M mini-batches of 2048, K=5 steps, 800 simulations per search in board games, 50 in Atari.
limits: Atari gains from planning are much smaller: performance plateaued at around 100 simulations, attributed to model inaccuracy.
agent_relevance: Search over a learned or LLM world model is only as good as that model; check model error before spending search budget.

source: Schrittwieser et al. (2020) MuZero
finding: A model trained with short searches kept improving with longer search at test time in Go.
numbers: Trained at about 0.1 s thinking time, tested up to 10 s; matched a perfect simulator.
quote: MuZero matched the performance of a perfect model, even when doing much larger searches
limits: Go only for this test; not shown for noisy language worlds.
agent_relevance: Test-time search budget may exceed the budget used when the value was learned, if the model is accurate.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized Planning with Large-Scale Transformers: A Case Study on Chess
finding: A 270M transformer trained to copy Stockfish 16 action values, with no search at test time, reached grandmaster blitz level against humans.
numbers: Lichess blitz Elo 2895 vs humans; tournament Elo 2299; puzzle accuracy 95.4% (270M), 94.5% (136M), 88.9% (9M); 10M games.
limits: Elo vs bots only 2299 (different pool; bots exploit weaknesses); labels come from Stockfish, so it distils search; blind to threefold repetition.
agent_relevance: Search results can be amortised into one-pass policy when strong labels exist; needs an oracle.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized Planning with Large-Scale Transformers: A Case Study on Chess
finding: Explicit search still helps RL-trained engines a lot; the searchless transformer nearly matches AlphaZero with MCTS on puzzles.
numbers: Puzzles: AlphaZero policy only 56.1%, value only 82.0%, 400 MCTS sims 95.6%; Leela policy only 88.6%, 400 sims 99.6%; Stockfish 16 (50ms) 99.8%; GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct 66.5%. Tournament Elo: AZ 400 sims 2470, Leela 400 sims 2858, Stockfish 50ms 2711.
limits: Supervised vs self-play training differ; puzzle accuracy is a narrow test.
agent_relevance: 400 simulations lift the same network from 56% to 96% on puzzles: search is a large multiplier when the raw policy is weak.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized Planning with Large-Scale Transformers: A Case Study on Chess
finding: Scale mattered in ablations, and the value-target choice mattered.
numbers: 9M: tournament Elo 2025; 136M: 2259; 270M: 2299. Behavioural cloning ablation 77.5% puzzles, lower than action-value targets (9M model).
limits: Ablations only at 9M; authors list repetition blindness and the Elo gap vs bots as limits.
agent_relevance: Predicting the value of all options trained a better chooser than copying the best move.

source: Schultz et al. (2025) Mastering Board Games by External and Internal Planning with Language Models
finding: A 2.7B language model (MAV) used as value, prior and world model inside external MCTS gained about 300 Elo with a small simulation budget.
numbers: Chess external Elo: MAV alone 2923 (mean scoring) or 2875 (max); MAV+MCTS 500 sims 3170, 1000 sims 3191; 100 sims already +68 internal Elo; gain grew logarithmically with simulations.
quote: Elo performance improves logarithmically as a function of the number of simulations
limits: Authors say the MCTS Elo estimates are not accurate (anchored to Stockfish blitz ratings); game data only, no natural language; needs engine-annotated training data.
agent_relevance: LM plus MCTS gives real, log-shaped gains; returns diminish, so S6 needs an explicit stop.

source: Schultz et al. (2025) Mastering Board Games by External and Internal Planning with Language Models
finding: Internal search (the model writes a minimax tree in its own output) also raised strength with budget, and the model built the requested tree shape almost always.
numbers: Tree shape correct 99.6% of 5980 positions; breadth up to 4, depth up to 2; Elo rose with tokens. Games were stopped at 1200+ centipawn advantage because the model shuffled pieces in won positions.
limits: Only shallow trees; needed fine-tuning on 40% search data, 20,000 steps, batch 512.
agent_relevance: In-context search works when trained for it; an untrained model should use code-run search (program decides transitions).

source: Schultz et al. (2025) Mastering Board Games by External and Internal Planning with Language Models
finding: MCTS with a learned prior beat plain MCTS with random rollouts, so the learned prior is the component that matters.
numbers: Basic MCTS baseline: uniform prior, random rollouts, 100 sims. Tournaments: 14689 games chess, 6334 Hex. Connect Four gain up to 244 Elo.
limits: Per-game table values garbled in the PDF text; only summary lines read.
agent_relevance: Rollouts from a random policy are a weak baseline.

source: Jones (2021) Scaling Scaling Laws with Board Games
finding: With AlphaZero on Hex, each extra order of magnitude of training compute lets you cut test-time search compute by about the same factor at equal strength.
numbers: 2,800 snapshots; frontiers fitted on small boards predict larger boards; prediction error decays exponentially as board sizes are added.
quote: for each extra order of magnitude of train-time compute, we can reduce test-time compute by a similar factor
limits: Hex, small boards; non-linear at the top and bottom of the curves; one author, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Search budget and model quality trade off; a better value model means less search.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: On MATH with PaLM 2-S*, verifier-guided beam search beat best-of-N at small budgets, but the gain faded and often reversed at large budgets.
numbers: Budgets 4, 16, 64, 256 generations. Lookahead search (k-step rollouts, MCTS-like) generally underperformed at equal generation budget. Compute-optimal allocation matched best-of-N with up to 4x less compute.
limits: One base model, one benchmark; the public PRM800K PRM was easily exploited, so they built their own automated PRM; lookahead costs extra.
agent_relevance: Search with a learned verifier over-optimises; pick search by difficulty.

source: Snell et al. (2024)
finding: On easy questions (levels 1-2) beam search got worse as budget grew, a sign of exploiting the reward model; on levels 3-4 it kept beating best-of-N; on level 5 nothing helped.
numbers: MATH difficulty bins, budgets 4-256.
limits: Predicted difficulty (PRM-based) weakens the benefit at high budget.
agent_relevance: The known game-AI failure (value error amplified by search) shows up in LLMs; gate search with a check, not the model's own score (G2, G5).

source: Snell et al. (2024)
finding: In a FLOPs-matched test, extra test-time compute on a smaller model beat a 14x larger model on easy and medium problems, but not on the hardest.
numbers: Against a 14x larger pretrained model; hardest bin: very little benefit from test-time compute.
limits: Depends on the ratio of inference to pretraining workload.
agent_relevance: Search substitutes for scale only where the small model already has a non-trivial success rate.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts
finding: On Game of 24 with GPT-4, tree search over thoughts with breadth 5 solved 74% versus 4% for chain of thought.
numbers: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC (k=100) 9.0%, CoT best of 100 49%, IO best of 100 33%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%. Crosswords word-level 60%, 4 of 20 games solved vs under 16% word-level for IO/CoT.
quote: ToT significantly enhances language models' problem-solving abilities
limits: Three tasks built to defeat GPT-4; GSM8K and StrategyQA subsets (100 each) gained little; GPT-3.5 + ToT 19%. Cost about 5.5k completion tokens per problem, near 100 CoT trials (6.7k).
agent_relevance: Even a fair best-of-100 CoT (49%) falls short, so structure beats raw sampling on search-shaped tasks.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts (Appendix B)
finding: Generator and evaluator quality both matter; a weaker generator hurt more than a weaker evaluator.
numbers: Game of 24: GPT-4 both 74%; GPT-4 generate + GPT-3.5 evaluate 64%; GPT-3.5 generate + GPT-4 evaluate 31%; GPT-3.5 both 19%. About 60% of CoT samples already failed after the first step.
limits: Single paper; prompts hand-tuned per task.
agent_relevance: The value function is a bottleneck; fits G5 (a judge is not a free check).

source: Feng et al. (2024) AlphaZero-Like Tree-Search can Guide LLM Decoding and Training (TS-LLM)
finding: A learned value function made tree search work across tasks; AlphaZero-style MCTS beat greedy baselines only where long-horizon planning mattered (RLHF alignment, chess endgame).
numbers: Tasks: GSM8K, Game24, PrOntoQA, RLHF, chess endgame; trees up to depth 64; learned LLaMA2-7B value beat prompted GPT-3.5 value in BFS Path@1.
limits: On shallow trees MCTS only matched baselines.
agent_relevance: Use tree search where depth matters; skip it for shallow reasoning.

source: Feng et al. (2024) AlphaZero-Like Tree-Search can Guide LLM Decoding and Training (TS-LLM)
finding: With matched compute, most of the advantage over self-consistency with a reward model vanished on GSM8K.
numbers: Equal-token comparison: TS-LLM advantage 'largely decrease' vs CoT-SC with ORM-vote on GSM8K, where only BFS greedy value search was best; tree search still dominated on the other four tasks. MCTS was almost the best of BFS-V, DFS-V and MCTS for multi-path search, showing value back-propagation matters.
quote: We are surprised to see that such simple algorithms can also have outstanding performance when compared fairly
limits: Authors say Path@1 comparisons are unfair because TS-LLM uses far more tokens.
agent_relevance: Always compare search to equal-token sample-and-select; unfair compute comparisons inflate tree search.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS)
finding: MCTS with external feedback and reflections reached 92.7% pass@1 on HumanEval with GPT-4 and a WebShop score of 75.9 with GPT-3.5.
numbers: HumanEval 92.7% (GPT-4); HotPotQA n=5 expansions, k=50 trajectories; code: 5 samples, 8 iterations.
limits: Authors say both search and semantic feedback are needed; ToT and RAP without observations were competitive with Reflexion; compute is high.
agent_relevance: Real external feedback (tests) inside the tree drives the result, consistent with G2 and G3.

source: Guan et al. (2025) rStar-Math
finding: Small models with MCTS and a process preference model, after 4 self-evolution rounds on 747k problems, matched or beat o1-preview on math.
numbers: MATH: Qwen2.5-Math-7B 58.8% to 90.0%; Phi3-mini 41.4% to 86.4% (o1-preview 85.5%); AIME 2024 53.3% (8/15); Olympiad Bench 65.6%; Omni-Math 50.5% vs o1-mini 60.5%.
limits: Needs trained policy and PPM; code-verified steps; lags o1-mini on Omni-Math.
agent_relevance: Search plus a verified-step value is strong, but the value is trained; our scaffold can use code checks only.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) ReST-MCTS*
finding: MCTS guided by an inferred process reward beat best-of-N and Tree-of-Thought at the same search budget and gave better self-training data.
numbers: Abstract-level claim: higher accuracy than Best-of-N and ToT at equal budget; beats ReST-EM and Self-Rewarding LM over iterations.
limits: Only abstract and intro read; per-benchmark numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Per-step value comes from outcome labels through search.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Adversarial Policies Beat Superhuman Go AIs
finding: An adversary trained with under 14% of KataGo's compute won over 97% against KataGo at superhuman search settings, and over 99% with no search, without playing Go well.
numbers: Win >97% at superhuman search; >99% no search; still wins more than half at 10 million visits per move; zero-shot transfer to Leela Zero, ELF OpenGo, Sai, Golaxy.
quote: they trick KataGo into making serious blunders that cause it to lose the game
limits: Gray-box access to the victim network. Human experts could copy the cyclic strategy to beat superhuman AIs.
agent_relevance: A searcher superhuman on average can have value-network blind spots that more search does not remove (G5).

source: Tseng et al. (2025) Can Go AIs be Adversarially Robust?
finding: Three defenses (adversarial training on hand-made positions, iterated adversarial training, a new architecture) all failed against freshly trained adversaries.
numbers: Original adversary 97% vs KataGo at 4096 visits; after defence a fine-tuned adversary won 47%; gift-adversary 91% vs dec23-victim (512 visits); continuous-adversary 65% at 4096; big-adversary 56% vs may24-victim at 65,536 visits; final iterated adversary a9 won 42% vs v9 at 65,536 visits with 26% of v9's compute.
limits: Win rate falls as victim visits rise, so search does help; but a patch for one attack leaves the class open (mostly cyclic-group attacks).
agent_relevance: Patching a seen failure is not robustness; only held-out attacks test it (G3).

source: McIlroy-Young et al. (2020) Aligning Superhuman AI with Human Behavior: Chess as a Model System (Maia)
finding: Strong engines predict human moves poorly; Maia (AlphaZero net trained on human games, no search) predicted human moves above 50%.
numbers: Stockfish matches human moves 33-41% (depth 15 best; depth 1 beats depth 5); Maia 46% to over 52%; each Maia peaks near its training rating; 10 MCTS rollouts degraded move-matching; 12 plies of history improved it.
quote: it tends to degrade move prediction performance in our setting
limits: Lichess data; no search by design, so no strength claim; move-matching is not outcome quality.
agent_relevance: Searching for the best move moves an agent away from human-like moves; useful to model a person, not to find truth.

source: Karvonen (2024) Emergent World Models and Latent Variable Estimation in Chess-Playing Language Models
finding: A GPT trained on chess PGN text learned a linear board-state code and estimated player skill; adding a skill vector raised win rate up to 2.6 times.
numbers: 25M and 50M parameter models (8 and 16 layers); linear probes on 13 piece types per square.
limits: Small models, not grandmaster strength; earlier Othello work failed on human-game data.
agent_relevance: LMs can track game state without search; code-tracked state is still safer.

source: Lehnert et al. (2024) Beyond A*: Searchformer
finding: A transformer trained on A* search traces solved 93.7% of unseen Sokoban tasks with up to 26.8% fewer search steps than A*, beating a solution-only model.
numbers: Trace training lengthened output 10x to 100x yet improved held-out performance; 5-10x smaller model and 10x less data than baselines.
limits: Synthetic mazes and Sokoban; a trained model, not a prompt.
agent_relevance: Search steps in the output help a trained model; for a prompted agent the trace must be checked.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: Using the LLM as a world model inside MCTS improved plan generation and math reasoning over chain of thought.
numbers: Abstract: RAP with LLaMA-33B surpasses CoT with GPT-4 on plan generation (figures not extracted).
limits: Only abstract and intro read.
agent_relevance: Same idea as TS-LLM; model errors compound with depth.
